analysis.one_liner: Requires pharmacy benefit managers to disclose all compensation to employer health plans.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to force pharmacy benefit managers to disclose their compensation to employers sits in the Senate health committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill amends an employee-benefits law (ERISA) so that pharmacy benefit managers and third-party administrators serving employer health plans must disclose direct and indirect compensation to the employers that sponsor the plans. Indirect compensation includes money PBMs keep from drugmaker rebates or from the gap between what a plan pays and what a pharmacy receives. The Labor Department would have to write clarifying rules within 180 days, and the bill states this merely clarifies requirements already in effect since the No Surprises Act.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and families with employer-sponsored health insurance benefit indirectly, because employers who can see the full compensation a PBM receives — including rebate money and pricing spreads — are better positioned to negotiate lower costs. Employers themselves, who legally act as fiduciaries for these plans, gain the information they need to evaluate their vendors. Community pharmacists could benefit indirectly if disclosure exposes spread pricing.

how_it_helps.text: Adds pharmacy benefit management services and third-party administration services to the list of services under ERISA section 408(b)(2) whose direct and indirect compensation must be disclosed to employer health plan fiduciaries, closing a gap PBMs have used to argue their fees do not have to be fully reported.

The disclosure obligation explicitly covers indirect compensation — which in the PBM business means money retained from drugmaker rebates or kept as the spread between what an employer's plan pays and what the pharmacy is reimbursed — not just the flat fees on the invoice.

The Labor Department must issue regulations within 180 days of enactment clarifying the disclosure requirements, with the rules applying to plan years starting at least 6 months later, so the change has a deadline rather than depending on voluntary action.

Employers sponsoring health plans — who are legally responsible as fiduciaries for spending plan money wisely — get a clearer picture of what their PBM is actually being paid, which is the starting point for negotiating it down.

analysis.who_pays: Pharmacy benefit managers and their corporate parents (CVS Caremark, Express Scripts, Optum Rx) and third-party administrators, whose affiliated and indirect revenue would become visible to the employers that pay them. Any compliance cost of producing the disclosures falls on these service providers, and if disclosure leads employers to renegotiate, their revenue from rebate retention and spread pricing would shrink.

drawbacks.text: The bill only requires disclosure to plan fiduciaries; it does not cap prices, ban spread pricing, restrict rebate practices, or guarantee any savings — workers only benefit if employers actually use the information to renegotiate.

The bill's own 'sense of Congress' says it imposes no requirement beyond rules already in effect since the No Surprises Act, framing it as a clarification; if regulators or courts already covered PBMs, the practical change may be small and depend heavily on how the Labor Department writes its regulations.

Producing detailed direct and indirect compensation reports imposes administrative costs on service providers, costs that in a competitive market are typically passed into the fees employers and plans pay.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This is a modest, low-cost transparency measure, not a price fix. Its honest case is that employers cannot negotiate away compensation they cannot see, and PBMs have argued their services fall outside ERISA's disclosure rules. Its honest limit is that disclosure alone changes nothing by itself: there is no cap on what PBMs can keep, no ban on the practices that generate hidden compensation, and no direct benefit to workers unless their employer acts on the information. The 'sense of Congress' language, by insisting this changes nothing new, also gives industry room to argue in implementation that nothing has really changed.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in December 2025 and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Senator Roger Marshall introduced the PBM Disclosure Act on December 4, 2025, joined at introduction by Senator Lisa Blunt Rochester, making the sponsorship bipartisan from the start.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, the standard first step that places it under that committee's control.
No further action appears in the record: the committee has not held a hearing, voted the bill out, or scheduled it, and the full Senate has not considered it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained and no one has lost — but if the bill dies quietly in committee, pharmacy benefit managers will be the clear winners, since the disclosure of their rebate and spread revenue would never take effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; PBMs if it dies

for.name: Roger Marshall
for.what_they_did: Introduced the PBM Disclosure Act and referred it to the Senate health committee.

for.name: Lisa Blunt Rochester
for.what_they_did: Joined the introduction as the bill's cosponsor, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

against.name: Bill Cassidy
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled a hearing, markup, or committee vote on the bill since its referral.

against.name: Pharmacy benefit manager industry (PCMA)
against.what_they_did: The PBM industry has a long record of lobbying against disclosure mandates that would expose rebate and spread revenue; no opposition to this specific bill appears in the congressional record.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced jointly by a Republican sponsor and its sole cosponsor, a Democrat, but with no votes yet there is no record of how the parties would split.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers (CVS Caremark, Express Scripts, Optum Rx)
industries.note: The bill adds PBM services to the compensation-disclosure rules, forcing PBMs to show employers the direct and indirect money they make — including retained rebates and pricing spreads. That visibility threatens a core part of PBM revenue, which is why the industry has historically fought transparency requirements.

industries.industry: Third-party administrators of employee health plans
industries.note: TPAs are covered by the same disclosure requirement, so they too would have to report all direct and indirect compensation from the plans they administer.

industries.industry: Large employers that sponsor health plans
industries.note: Employers acting as plan fiduciaries receive fuller compensation information, which strengthens their hand when negotiating PBM contracts and lowers the legal risk of overpaying vendors.

The bill does not regulate drugmakers, but disclosure of how much rebate money PBMs retain could expose the rebate system manufacturers rely on to protect list prices, creating indirect pressure on that arrangement.

analysis.trajectory: The bill's prospects are those of any newly introduced Senate bill with two sponsors: most die in committee. Its realistic paths are a HELP Committee hearing on PBM practices, inclusion as a provision in a larger health-cost or drug-pricing package, or attention during a broader PBM reform push. Bipartisan anger at PBMs is one of the few issues with momentum in both parties, which gives it a plausible — but not likely — route to being attached to must-pass legislation before the 119th Congress ends in January 2027.
